# Isaiah 33: verse-by-verse research notes

**Coverage:** I read Guzik (Enduring Word), the Pulpit Commentary, Gill, Matthew Henry, Barnes, the Cambridge Bible, the Expositor's Bible, Wesley and Spurgeon. I didn't reach any netbible.org, bibleodyssey.org, Catholic, Orthodox, or prosperity/word‑of‑faith/hyper‑grace pages on this chapter, so those sections are left out. The nearest thing to modern scholarship comes from the older critical commentaries on biblehub (Cambridge, Expositor's).

**Setting (most sources):** Most commentators place the chapter during Sennacherib's invasion of Judah. Matthew Henry says it covers the distress of Judah and Jerusalem by Sennacherib's invasion and their deliverance out of that distress by the destruction of the Assyrian army. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Isa/Isa_033.cfm. Gill reads it more broadly, as an account of God's judgments upon the enemies of his people, and of the peaceable, comfortable, and happy state of the church in the latter day. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/33.htm

---

**v. 1**
- **Traditional:** The Pulpit Commentary says the destroyer is evidently, Assyria - the world-power of this entire group of prophecies. It explains that conquerors can't safely stop, because their aggressions have roused so many enmities that, let them cease to attack, and at once they are attacked in their turn. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/33.htm
- Guzik links the verse to Matthew 7:1–2, saying God has every right to deal with us as we have dealt with others. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-33/
- Henry notes that the Assyrian dealt treacherously with those that had always dealt faithfully with him. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Isa/Isa_033.cfm
- Barnes says the treachery was this: Judah had asked Assyria for help against Syria and Samaria, and Assyria had taken occasion from that invitation to bring desolation on Judah. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/isaiah-33.html
- **A Protestant difference (Gill, Baptist):** Gill grants that Sennacherib is more probable than Nebuchadnezzar, but he thinks it seems best to interpret it of the Romish antichrist. He reads the whole chapter this way. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/33-1.html
- **Other views:** Gill also reports the Jewish commentator Kimchi's view: if the verse is about the Messiah's time, the destroyer is a future king of nations, which Kimchi ties to Persia in Daniel. Another scholar, Vitringa, applied it to Antiochus Epiphanes and the Maccabean period. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/33-1.html

**v. 2**
- The Pulpit Commentary notes that the mingling of prayer with prophecy is very unusual, and indicative of highly excited feeling. "Every morning" means continually, day by day, since their need of thy support is continual. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/33.htm
- The Cambridge Bible says the writer speaks for the whole community, something Isaiah rarely does (see Isaiah 32:15); nowhere, as here, in a prayer. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/isaiah/33.htm
- Guzik: God's people no longer look to the Egyptians, they no longer look to themselves. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-33/
- Henry: we must every morning commit ourselves to him, and go forth in his strength to do the work of the day. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/isaiah/33.htm

**v. 3**
- The Pulpit Commentary says "the peoples" are the contingents from many nations which made up the huge army of Sennacherib. The "thunder" is the noise God makes as he rises up (it cites Ps 29). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/33.htm
- Gill reads the verse either as a prayer ("let the people flee") or as a prediction ("they shall flee"). He applies it to Christ's armies going out against the beast and the false prophet. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/33.htm

**v. 4**
- The Pulpit Commentary says the Bible's account of the Assyrian defeat doesn't mention plunder. But it holds that a defeated army must have [left] an enormous booty left behind. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/33.htm
- Guzik quotes Bultema: Jerusalem's people probably congregated like caterpillars around the corpses and the implements of war. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-33/
- Barnes says the word translated "caterpillar" properly denotes the devourer, and is applied usually to a species of locust. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/isaiah-33.html

**v. 5**
- The Pulpit Commentary: destroying the Assyrian army is an exaltation of God; i.e. it causes him to be exalted in the thoughts of those who have cognizance of the fact. It sees Judah's deliverance as partly the result, and partly the cause, of the people turning back to God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/33.htm
- Ellicott: the prophet's vision takes in the ideal city of God. https://biblehub.com/isaiah/33-5.htm
- Guzik: the people give thanks before the answer comes. You can, by faith, give Him thanks ahead of time. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-33/
- Gill applies the verse to Zion as the church, where his word shall be faithfully preached, and his ordinances duly administered. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/33-5.html

**v. 6**
- The Pulpit Commentary translates the verse literally as the stability of thy times shall be (i.e. consist in) a rich store of salvations, wisdom, and knowledge. It says the wisdom meant is the kind grounded in "the fear of the Lord" (Ps 111:10). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/33.htm
- The Cambridge Bible: a right religious attitude is the true strength of the nation and the pledge of its deliverance from all dangers. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/isaiah/33.htm
- **Whose treasure?** Commentators disagree about who "his" refers to in "his treasure."
  - Gill lists three options: Hezekiah's treasure, the Lord's treasure, or best of all, the church's treasure, and every true believer's. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/33-6.html
  - Guzik says the fear of the Lord is a gift God gives us, not so we will cower in fear, but so we will rightly honor Him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-33/
  - Henry: true piety is the only treasure which can never be plundered or spent. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/isaiah/33.htm

**v. 7**
- The word translated "valiant ones" is a puzzle. Barnes says it has given great perplexity to expositors. It occurs nowhere else in the Scriptures. He thinks they were Jewish envoys sent to Sennacherib to ask for peace terms. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/isaiah-33.html
- Guzik quotes Adam Clarke: the Jewish commentator Kimchi thought the word was the name of the angel who struck the Assyrian camp, while the Vulgate (the old Latin Bible) translates it "seers." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-33/
- The Pulpit Commentary reads it literally as "lions of God." It thinks the "envoys of peace" were Hezekiah's embassies to Sennacherib (2 Kgs 18:14–17). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/33.htm

**v. 8**
- The Pulpit Commentary: Sennacherib took Hezekiah's payment and then attacked anyway, so Isaiah, therefore, taxes him with having broken his covenant. "Regards no man" means he pays no attention to protests. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/33.htm
- Gill applies the verse to the Roman antichrist invading Protestant lands. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/33.htm

**v. 9**
- The Pulpit Commentary calls Lebanon, Sharon, Carmel and Bashan the four most beautiful regions of the Holy Land. It sees them withering both from Assyrian raids and as if mourning with Judah. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/33.htm
- The Cambridge Bible says "the earth" here is closest to what we would call "Nature," and prefers "shake off their leaves" to "their fruits." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/isaiah/33.htm
- Gill reads the withered places as the church robbed of its ministers. He names Great Britain as one fruitful region that will become like a desert. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/33.htm

**v. 10**
- The Pulpit Commentary: Judah's extremity is Jehovah's opportunity. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/33.htm
- Guzik: as the whole earth is brought low, the Lord lifts himself up. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-33/

**v. 11**
- The Pulpit Commentary: Assyria's plans are chaff that will come to nothing, and the enemy's own fury becomes the fire that destroys them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/33.htm
- Gill reads "your breath" as "your spirit": pride, rage and blasphemy that bring God's fire on the enemy. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/33.htm

**v. 12**
- The Pulpit Commentary: lime and thorns are things fire burns up completely and quickly. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/33.htm
- Guzik quotes Motyer: the picture of burning lime stresses the intensity of the blaze. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-33/

**v. 13**
- The Pulpit Commentary: God calls the nations near and far to recognise his power, as shown in the judgment on Assyria. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/33.htm
- Henry takes "far off" to mean far off in place or in time: Let distant regions and future ages hear what God has done. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/33-16.html

**v. 14**
- The Pulpit Commentary: sinners in Zion now see God as "a consuming fire" (Deut 4:24), whose next outbreak may be upon themselves, and will shudder at the prospect. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/33.htm
- The Cambridge Bible says the questions are not just rhetorical, like the similar questions in Psalm 15. They are spoken by the frightened sinners themselves. The word "dwell" means strictly "sojourn as a protected guest," https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/isaiah/33.htm
- **Does the verse speak of eternal punishment?**
  - Barnes thinks the speakers had a belief of the doctrine of eternal punishment. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/isaiah-33.html
  - Henry: it is the wrath of an ever-living God preying on the conscience of a never-dying soul. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/isaiah/33.htm
- The Biblical Illustrator gives a softer reading: The fire of God is the fire of love as well as the fire of purity. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/isaiah-33.html
- **Gill (historicist reading):** Gill thinks the "sinners in Zion" are probably formal professors, and hypocritical persons, in the reformed churches, or else the antichrist's own followers. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/33.htm

**v. 15**
- The Pulpit Commentary counts six marks of the upright person: just conduct, honest speech, hatred of oppression, refusing bribes, shutting the ear to murderous plots, and shutting the eye to sinful sights. It says the list targets the favorite sins of the time. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/33.htm
- The Cambridge Bible compares Psalms 15 and 24. It points out that the verb in "shakes his hands" is the same one used in v. 9 for trees shaking off their leaves. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/isaiah/33.htm
- **Works and grace (Protestant emphases):**
  - Gill (Baptist, Calvinist) reads "walks righteously" as walking by faith on Christ as his righteousness. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/33-15.html
  - Spurgeon (Baptist) says the Holy Ghost must regenerate you; otherwise, you cannot walk uprightly. https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/a-precious-promise-for-a-pure-people
  - Henry stresses guarding the senses: such people must stop their ears to temptations, and turn away their eyes from beholding vanity. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/33-18.html

**v. 16**
- The Pulpit Commentary reads "dwell on the heights" as living in God's presence, and "his food will be provided" as everything needed for life. It adds that godliness has the promise of the life that now is as well as the life to come (1 Tim 4:8). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/33.htm
- Gill spiritualises the verse: Christ is the "place of defence" and the bread of life. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/33-16.html
- The Biblical Illustrator says the promise of bread is also literally true. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/33-16.html

**v. 17**
- **Which king?** Most writers see both Hezekiah and the Messiah here.
  - Guzik: In the most immediate sense, this referred to Hezekiah; but in the ultimate sense, to our Beautiful Savior Jesus Christ. He calls this sight the greatest glory of heaven, and says Christ's scars are part of his beauty. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-33/
  - Spurgeon pictures Hezekiah gone up to the House of the Lord to return public thanks. He adds that "the King" here mentioned is a type of the Lord Jesus Christ. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/spurgeon/sermons57.viii.html
  - Spurgeon also rejects another reading: that the verse threatens exile, with the Jews seeing the Assyrian king in Nineveh. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/spurgeon/sermons57.viii.html
  - In a separate sermon he says You must see Him by faith in His sufferings or else you will never see Him by sight in His beauty. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/spurgeon/sermons13.xxv.html
- **The "land that stretches afar":**
  - The Pulpit Commentary takes the King as Messianic. It records that Lowth and Delitzsch translate the land as "Thine own land far extended," but argues that a Messianic King implies a world-wide land. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/33.htm
  - Gill reads it as the heavenly country, or else Christ's kingdom spread worldwide. He mentions that the Targum (an old Aramaic paraphrase) wrongly made it "the land of hell." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/33-17.html
- **Seeing Christ now, through the Church:** In a sermon by H. E. Manning collected in the Biblical Illustrator, Christ dwells among us in His Church really though invisibly, and through its Ordinances fulfils towards us the promise, even before heaven. https://biblehub.com/sermons/isaiah/33-17.htm

**v. 18**
- **Most read it as looking back on past fear:**
  - The Pulpit Commentary says the three officials are Assyrian: the scribe who recorded tribute, the officer who weighed it, and the engineer who counted the city's towers. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/33.htm
  - Wesley (Methodist) calls the verse a thankful acknowledgment of deliverance from their former terrors and miseries. Unlike the Pulpit Commentary, he makes the officials Judah's own war officers. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/33-18.html
  - Clarke (Methodist) agrees with the Pulpit Commentary that the scribe was Assyrian, appointed to assess Judah for heavy taxes. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/33-18.html
- **Guzik differs:** he applies the verse to people set against God, for whom the King's appearing will be the greatest terror. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-33/

**v. 19**
- The Pulpit Commentary: this is the barbarous people - the Assyrians (compare 28:11). It adds that the generation which witnessed the destruction of Sennacherib's army probably did not see the Assyrians again. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/33.htm
- Guzik: Isaiah mixes the pictures of the LORD's ultimate deliverance on the day of judgment, and the soon coming deliverance from the Assyrians. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-33/

**v. 20**
- The Pulpit Commentary sees a possible reference to Sennacherib's threat to deport the city, a threat that would not come true. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/33.htm
- Henry reads the tent as the church: The promises of the covenant are its stakes, which shall never be removed, and the ordinances and institutions of the gospel are its cords. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Isa/Isa_033.cfm
- Jamieson, Fausset & Brown: Christ's Church shall never fall. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Isa/Isa_033.cfm

**v. 21**
- The Expositor's Bible: Assyria and Egypt had their great rivers for defence, but Judah's defence is God himself, without sign of battle. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/isaiah/33.htm
- Guzik quotes Grogan's picture of Jerusalem as a kind of Near Eastern Venice or Amsterdam. He also quotes Poole: the river protects the city, yet no enemy ships can use it to attack. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-33/

**v. 22**
- Gill applies the three titles to Christ. He notes that the Targum relates them to the exodus and Sinai and to a future victory over Gog, which shows that the ancient Jews understood this prophecy as referring to times yet to come. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/33-22.html
- Henry: as protection draws allegiance, so allegiance may expect protection. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/33-16.html

**v. 23**
- **Whose ship?**
  - The Pulpit Commentary takes it as Judah: comparing God to a river leads to picturing Judah herself as a badly appointed ship. It translates "spread the sail" as "spread the ensign" (a flag). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/33.htm
  - Gill says most interpreters understand it of the Assyrians, pictured as a ship in distress. He applies the dividing of plunder to Protestants taking the spoil of the "Papists." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/33-23.html
- Guzik: Even the lame take the prey. God's deliverance comes in unexpected ways. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-33/

**v. 24**
- **Is the healing literal or spiritual?**
  - The Pulpit Commentary: There shall be no sickness in the restored Jerusalem at least, no "sickness unto death." It adds that the prophet floats off into Messianic anticipations. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/33.htm
  - Henry: Sickness is taken away in mercy, when the fruit of it is the taking away of sin. If iniquity be taken away, we have little reason to complain of outward affliction. He points the verse ultimately to heaven. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/isaiah/33.htm
- The Expositor's Bible says that if this is Isaiah's last oracle, we have the literal crown of all his prophesying in these two words: forgiven iniquity. It adds that forgiveness does not change the outside of life, since Assyria still returned to besiege the city. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/isaiah/33.htm
- Guzik quotes Poole: beyond the rescue from Assyria lies the pardon of all their sins. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/isaiah/isaiah-33.cfm

---

**Note on modern scholarship:** The Cambridge Bible hints at an authorship question about vv. 5–6, saying that if he is the author, Isaiah is anticipating a coming change in the nation's character. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/isaiah/33.htm. The Expositor's Bible dates the chapter to 701 BC, a few months after chapter 22, and says critics unite in that placement. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/isaiah/33.htm
